notes.meaning: God describes the land given to the northern tribes, beginning with Dan at the far northern border. Dan receives a wide strip running all the way from the eastern border to the Mediterranean Sea in the west. Even though Dan had fallen into idolatry in past history, God graciously gives them a full share in the land.

differ.view: Some evangelicals understand these borders as a literal division of the land of Israel during a future thousand-year reign of Christ on earth.

notes.meaning: Asher receives the next strip of territory just south of Dan, stretching from east to west. Each tribal allotment spans the full width of the land in an orderly, parallel fashion. This balanced layout shows that God provides equitably for all His people.

Naphtali is assigned the strip directly south of Asher, running from the eastern boundary to the western sea. Like Dan and Asher, Naphtali was descended from a servant of Jacob's wives and sits on the outer edge of the country. Even the less prominent tribes receive their rightful place in God's plan.

Manasseh is allotted the next strip of territory south of Naphtali, reaching across from east to west. In the past, half of Manasseh lived east of the Jordan River and half lived on the west side. In this renewed land, Manasseh is fully united within the main borders.

Ephraim receives the strip bordering Manasseh from the eastern border to the west. Ephraim and Manasseh were both sons of Joseph, and each receives a full tribal portion. This arrangement fulfills the double blessing given to the family of Joseph.

Reuben is given the land bordering Ephraim from east to west. Reuben had lost his rights as the firstborn son in ancient times and originally settled outside the Promised Land east of the Jordan. Here, his past failures are pardoned, and he receives an inheritance alongside his brothers.

Judah receives the strip directly south of Reuben, extending from east to west. Judah was the royal tribe that produced King David and the promised Messiah. Because of this special role, Judah is given an honoured spot right next to the central holy district.

South of Judah lies a special section of land twenty-five thousand cubits wide that must be set apart for the Lord. It matches the length of the other tribal strips from east to west. At the very center of this sacred tract sits the holy sanctuary, or temple.

The special holy portion given directly to the Lord measures twenty-five thousand cubits long and ten thousand cubits wide. It provides space for the temple and homes for the priests who lead worship. It marks the spiritual center of the whole restored nation.

This holy district belongs to the priests to give them a peaceful place to live. It forms a large rectangle measuring twenty-five thousand cubits on the north and south, and ten thousand cubits on the east and west. The temple of the Lord stands directly in the middle of this area.

This land is reserved for the priests descended from Zadok. They remained faithful and obedient when the rest of Israel and the other Levites turned away to worship idols. God notices and rewards those who stay true to Him when others wander.

This tract is considered most holy and belongs entirely to the faithful priests. It borders the territory given to the other Levites. Its special sacred status keeps common activities far away from God's presence.

Next to the priests' territory, the other Levites receive an area of equal size. It measures twenty-five thousand cubits long and ten thousand cubits wide. The Levites use this land while they assist the priests and take care of the temple courts.

The Levites are strictly forbidden from selling, trading, or transferring any part of this land. Because it is dedicated as firstfruits to the Lord, it is permanently holy. Holy gifts given for God's service must never be treated as private property.

The remaining strip of five thousand cubits wide and twenty-five thousand cubits long is set apart for common city use. Here, common simply means ordinary daily life, such as houses and pastures, rather than temple rituals. The city itself sits right in the middle of this section.
The city itself forms a four-sided square within this common area. Each of its four sides measures exactly four thousand five hundred cubits. Its neat, balanced design shows divine order and harmony.

An open border of pastureland surrounds the city, extending two hundred and fifty cubits on every side. This creates a green belt around the homes and walls. It provides open space and grazing room for the livestock of the community.

Farmland extends ten thousand cubits to the east and ten thousand cubits to the west of the city area. This ground runs alongside the holy district. The crops grown here supply daily food for the people who live and work in the city.

Workers from all twelve tribes of Israel come to farm this land and serve the city. The city does not belong to any single tribe, so no group can claim superiority over the others. All God's people share equal responsibility in caring for their common community.

When the areas for the priests, the Levites, and the city are joined together, they form a perfect square. The entire holy district measures twenty-five thousand cubits on each of its four sides. This balanced shape represents completeness, unity, and lasting stability.

The land to the east and west of the holy square belongs to the ruler, known as the prince. His property reaches all the way to the outer borders, while the holy district and sanctuary remain protected in the center. Giving the prince his own ample estate prevents him from seizing the people's land.

The land of the Levites and the city area sit right in the middle of the prince's estate. The whole district lies between the borders of Judah in the north and Benjamin in the south. This arrangement keeps the civic and religious center well defended and supported.

Benjamin receives the first tribal strip south of the holy district, stretching across from east to west. In Israel's history, Benjamin remained loyal to David alongside Judah. Both faithful tribes are honored by being placed right next to God's holy dwelling place.

Simeon is allotted the strip just south of Benjamin, running from east to west. In older times, Simeon did not have its own unified territory and was swallowed up inside Judah. Here, Simeon is restored and given an independent portion among the tribes.
Issachar receives the strip bordering Simeon, reaching all the way from the eastern border to the sea. God ensures that every family in Israel has a secure home and an equal share in the land.

Zebulun receives the next strip of territory south of Issachar from east to west. Rather than living only on the seacoast as before, Zebulun now shares the same straight, uniform portion as the other tribes.

Gad is allotted the southernmost tribal portion, bordering Zebulun from east to west. Gad once chose land outside Canaan proper on the east side of the Jordan. In God's new order, Gad is brought safely into the heart of the promised country.
The southern border of Gad marks the southern boundary of the whole country. It runs from Tamar south to the waters of Meribath-kadesh, follows the Brook of Egypt, and ends at the Mediterranean Sea.

The Lord declares that this is how the land will be divided among the twelve tribes of Israel. Every tribe is restored and granted a lasting inheritance. God keeps His ancient promises and never forgets any part of His family.

differ.view: Some Baptists take these tribal inheritances spiritually, picturing the secure place and privileges believers have in Christ's church.
Some evangelicals teach that ethnic Israel will literally inherit these exact tracts of land during a future millennium on earth.

notes.meaning: The description turns back to the city to measure its outer walls and gates. The north side of the city measures four thousand five hundred cubits long. These measurements highlight the clear boundaries and open access of the community.

The city gates are named after the twelve tribes of Israel, showing that the whole nation has an open door into the city. The three northern gates, facing toward the temple, are named for Reuben, Judah, and Levi. These three sons of Leah represent seniority, royalty, and the priesthood.

The east wall also measures four thousand five hundred cubits and contains three gates. These gates are named for Joseph, Benjamin, and Dan. Naming a gate for Joseph covers Ephraim and Manasseh together, making room to honor Levi as one of the twelve.

The south wall measures four thousand five hundred cubits and has three gates. These gates are named for Simeon, Issachar, and Zebulun, who were all sons of Leah. Each side of the city continues the same balanced pattern.

The west wall also measures four thousand five hundred cubits, with gates for Gad, Asher, and Naphtali. This completes the four-sided perimeter of the city. Having open gates on all four sides shows that people can enter God's city from every direction.

The total perimeter around the four walls of the city is eighteen thousand cubits. From that time on, the city receives a glorious new name: The Lord Is There. God's presence, which had left Jerusalem earlier because of sin, now returns to dwell with His people forever.

differ.view: Reformed interpreters understand this city and its new name as a picture of the church of Jesus Christ, where God dwells by His Spirit, pointing forward to the perfection of heaven.
Some evangelicals hold that this refers to a literal rebuilt city of Jerusalem during an earthly thousand-year reign where Christ will rule in person.
Methodist commentators see the name as a promise of God's abiding presence among pure, faithful worshippers in gospel times.
